reference.source: Standard endocrinology reference texts and adrenal disorder consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A rare cause of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, typically in children and young adults, in which the adrenals contain small pigmented (dark brown to black) cortical micronodules
The glands are often normal-sized or only slightly enlarged on imaging, so cross-sectional scanning can appear deceptively unremarkable
Strongly associated with Carney complex, and most cases carry germline inactivating mutations in PRKAR1A, the regulatory subunit of protein kinase A
A characteristic feature is a paradoxical rise in urinary or serum cortisol during high-dose dexamethasone administration (Liddle test), rather than the expected suppression
Cushingoid features may be cyclical or atypical, and growth failure with weight gain in a child should prompt consideration of this diagnosis
Screening for other Carney complex manifestations (cardiac myxomas, spotty skin pigmentation, testicular and other endocrine tumours) is essential once PPNAD is suspected
Bilateral adrenalectomy is generally required because the disease is bilateral and driven by constitutive protein kinase A activation
reference.pathophysiology: PPNAD is a bilateral adrenocortical disorder in which numerous small cortisol-secreting micronodules, containing lipofuscin pigment, arise within an often atrophic surrounding cortex. Autonomous cortisol production suppresses pituitary ACTH. The molecular basis in most patients is a germline loss-of-function mutation in PRKAR1A, which encodes the type 1A regulatory subunit of protein kinase A; loss of this inhibitory subunit leads to constitutive, cAMP-independent activation of protein kinase A signalling and unregulated steroidogenesis. This dysregulated signalling also explains the paradoxical increase in cortisol seen with dexamethasone. The condition is a component of Carney complex, a multiple neoplasia and lentiginosis syndrome.
additionalInvestigations: 24-hour urinary free cortisol and late-night salivary cortisol to confirm hypercortisolism
Paired low plasma ACTH with failure to suppress on low-dose dexamethasone establishing ACTH independence
High-dose dexamethasone (Liddle) testing to elicit the paradoxical cortisol rise
Adrenal CT or MRI, recognising that glands may look near-normal despite active disease
PRKAR1A germline genetic testing and evaluation for Carney complex features
Echocardiography and dermatological review to detect cardiac myxomas and lentigines
redFlags: Cardiac myxoma causing embolic events or obstruction as part of Carney complex
Severe or cyclical hypercortisolism with growth arrest in a child
Family history suggesting an inherited multiple neoplasia syndrome
Post-adrenalectomy adrenal insufficiency requiring lifelong replacement
reference.prognosis: Cushing syndrome due to PPNAD is effectively cured by bilateral adrenalectomy, which necessitates lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement. Overall prognosis is dominated by other Carney complex manifestations, particularly cardiac myxomas, so lifelong surveillance is required.
pitfalls: Concluding the adrenals are normal because imaging shows no discrete mass
Interpreting a paradoxical cortisol rise on dexamethasone as an assay error rather than a diagnostic clue
Failing to screen for Carney complex and missing life-threatening cardiac myxomas
Not offering genetic counselling for an inheritable PRKAR1A-related condition
references: Consensus guidance on Carney complex and PPNAD
